newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-IMF/World Bank meetings preach to converted.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IMF/World Bank meetings preach to converted.

text.p: The annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund, which continue on Wednesday, are taking on the character of a religious revival gathering, with no one willing to question the path of the global economy.

From rich and poor, large and small, the litany has been the same: the global economy is entering a period of growing opportunity and well-being that provides a stepping off place to deal with issues that had seemed almost insurmountable.
Problems that were once only whispered about, such as entrenched corruption in many countries, were being discussed openly in the belief they can be solved.

World Bank President James Wolfensohn on Tuesday lashed out at corruption in industrial and developing countries, calling it a cancer and vowing not to tolerate it in the projects his organization finances.
"Corruption is a problem that all countries have to confront," he told policymakers from the bank's 181 member nations. "We need to deal with the cancer of corruption."

By throwing a spotlight on a problem that traditionally has been downplayed, the plain-speaking Wolfensohn risked raising hackles in developing nations where his broadside may be viewed as an attempt to meddle.

In the past, these meetings have hardly been cozy affairs. Those left out of the global economic dream have complained bitterly that the industrial countries were not doing enough to improve their condition.
The joint IMF and World Bank Development Committee, a forum where rich and poor countries can chew over differences, has often been the scene of frustration on both sides.

The industrial countries as well as the IMF have complained that poor nations refused to take the painful medicine of reforms such as opening their markets, cutting runaway budget deficits and reducing subsidies.

This week's decision to go ahead with a multi-billion dollar plan to help the poorest countries unload a portion of their unsustainable debt may once have ended in bitterness on both sides, with donors calling the deal too expensive and debtors saying it was not enough.
But the outcome in the Development Committee was almost unprecedented as both sides hailed the agreement.
Wolfensohn went so far as to call the debt reduction plan's reception a "lovefest."
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is expected on Wednesday to repeat again the current economic orthodoxy when he speaks to the plenary session.
The United States, Rubin will likely say, has tightened its belt and has produced a big payoff in growth, low inflation and unemployment.
